title: Why training fades, and how to make it stick

audience.who: employees and people managers back from a workshop or course
audience.knows: what it feels like to forget training; no memory science
audience.cares_about: not wasting the time they spent in training, looking capable afterwards

outcome: Right after their next training, the viewer schedules three short self-tests at growing gaps and does them instead of rereading their notes
through_line: Forgetting is the default, and the fix is not more study time: it is pulling the idea back out of your head, a little later each time

arc_plan.what: One person leaves a great Monday workshop; by Friday most of it has gone quiet. We watch it happen before we name it.
In about four minutes the viewer will have a schedule they can use after their very next training
Start from what every viewer has felt: knowing something on the day and blanking on it a week later
Name the forgetting curve (the early researcher who measured it on himself), show its shape: steep at first, then flattening
Refute the tempting fix: rereading feels like learning because the page looks familiar, but familiar is not the same as recallable
Show what does work: each self-test pulls the memory back up and the next drop is slower; spacing the tests makes each one count more
The viewer decides which of two plans for the same training keeps more a month later, then hears why the tempting one loses
A worked schedule: after a day, after a few days, after a week or two, each test a few minutes long
Back to the same person after her next workshop, using the schedule; the pocket rule the viewer keeps

must_cover.what: the forgetting curve: forgetting is fastest soon after learning and then slows
who first measured it and roughly when, stated only as the knowledge sheet states it
retrieval practice beats rereading, and why rereading feels effective anyway
spacing: reviews spread out over time beat the same reviews crammed together
a practical expanding schedule, framed as a guideline rather than magic numbers
a concrete plan the viewer can apply to the next training they attend

must_avoid: percentages of forgetting presented as universal facts
jargon before the viewer has seen the idea
more than one metaphor for memory
example_posture: One invented but ordinary colleague followed across days, clearly framed as illustrative ('say', 'meet'); workplace training only (a workshop, a course), no school or exam examples.
visual_direction: A friendly character whose thoughts visibly fade over the week; the curve drawn as a line that drops and then recovers after each self-test; a value that drains and refills; a journey across days on a calendar; a side-by-side of rereading versus testing; a short checklist to keep.
voice_note: A warm senior colleague, practical and unhurried; shows before naming; one gentle heads-up before the rereading trap; never preachy.
open_questions: Should the presenter at the start and end be named, or stay an unnamed guide?
Will the video sit in an LMS where a real quiz could replace the in-video pause?

inferred: must_avoid entries beyond the requester's 'avoid popular myths'
